pullRequestsFalamPouco.subtitle: A story about AI, Jira, GitHub and development maturity
pullRequestsFalamPouco.content:
# When Pull Requests Said Too Little ### _A story about AI, Jira, GitHub and development maturity_
It was just another Tuesday, one of those days when the team was already at its delivery limit. A new PR appeared in the repository: generic title, shallow description, no context. The reviewing developer looked at the code like someone facing a puzzle without a reference picture. And QA? Had to guess whether what arrived for testing actually matched what Jira requested. It was the portrait of a flawed process, where haste swallowed clarity. ## The Problem The team faced a common dilemma: PRs with superficial descriptions. This made **code review almost blind**. Without understanding the motivation for the change, reviewers wasted time, QAs tested in the dark, and gaps went unnoticed. The result? Rework, production failures, and accumulated frustration. ## The Turning Point: Unite AI, Jira and GitHub Then came the idea to automate the process. What if an AI could **cross-reference data from Jira, GitHub and branches**, delivering a complete, structured and contextualized description for each PR? The proposal was bold: - The dev chose the branch on GitHub. - Selected the corresponding Jira card. - The tool, with integrated AI, generated a **robust description** in the team's standard format: title, motivation, changes made, impact, recommendations and implementation verification. With no additional effort, what was once a bottleneck transformed into **a clear, objective and reliable flow**. ## Technical Choices To build this automator, some decisions proved crucial: - **Integration with GitHub and Jira APIs**, to collect branches and active tasks from the dev. - **AI processing layer**, responsible for transforming raw data into fluid and detailed text. - **Simple interface**, guiding the developer intuitively. - **Automatic standardization of descriptions**, eliminating variations and ensuring consistency in PRs. More than code, it was necessary to **think about team experience**: it wasn't about creating a new system, but adding without hindering. ## Results The change was felt quickly: - Reviewers gained **total clarity** about what they were evaluating. - QA gained **confidence** in testing, knowing exactly what to validate. - Developers freed themselves from the burden of writing complex descriptions under pressure. - And the team, as a whole, took a leap in **maturity** in their delivery process. ## Final Reflection More than automating descriptions, the project showed that AI can be a powerful ally for development teams. It doesn't replace human critical thinking, but **opens space for that thinking to be more precise and productive**. It was an important step towards a more transparent, secure and efficient software engineering process. Because, in the end, every team deserves their PRs to tell complete stories — not just loose sentences.

porTrasDaIa.subtitle: A technical dive into integrations, prompts and models that transformed the development workflow
porTrasDaIa.content:
# Behind the Automation: How We Built Intelligent PRs with AI ### _A technical dive into integrations, prompts and models that transformed the development workflow_
After telling the story of how AI helped our team mature its processes, it's time to open the technical backstage. In this post, we'll talk about **how the backend was built**, which integrations became vital, and why we opted for **two different AI models** to ensure quality and clarity in Pull Requests. ## Backend Architecture The project was born with the idea of being modular. Each service has its clear responsibility: - **GithubService** → responsible for creating and updating PRs, as well as interacting with branches and commits. - **IssuesService** → integrates with Jira, bringing title, description and status of the selected issue. - **PrService** → organizes the complete flow: collects data, calls the AI and publishes the PR on GitHub. - **OllamaService** → connects the backend to AI models, handling prompts and post-processing. This separation brought scalability and ease of maintenance, allowing each part to evolve without breaking the whole. ## The Flow Between Jira, GitHub and AI The automation cycle happens in four stages: 1. The dev selects the branch and issue. 2. The backend collects raw information from Jira and GitHub. 3. The dev requests PR creation. 4. The backend organizes the prompt with information for technical analysis. 5. When technical analysis finishes, the prompt is assembled for PR text creation based on technical analysis. 6. The result returns formatted in the team's standard and is published on GitHub. This simple pipeline hides a strategic choice: **use two models instead of one**. ## Two Models, Two Roles Using just one model seemed the easier path, but results showed inconsistency: wordy descriptions or shallow analyses. That's when we decided to separate functions: 1. **codellama** → focuses on technical code analysis, suggesting improvements, identifying bugs and maintaining repository standards. 2. **phi4-mini** → acts as a "technical writer", transforming codellama's recommendations into clear, objective and understandable descriptions. This division brought **clarity and consistency**, preventing a single model from being overloaded. ### Prompt Examples - Prompt sent to codellama: ```ts ### CONTEXT AND RULES ### You are a Staff Engineer with over 10 years of experience in forensic code analysis and pull request reviews. Your task is to RIGOROUSLY verify if Jira requirements were ACTUALLY implemented in the code, without assumptions. **MANDATORY RULES**: 1. NEVER mention files, classes or methods that are not EXPLICITLY present in the provided commits. 2. If there is no clear evidence, classify as **NOT IMPLEMENTED** and explain why. 3. FOR EACH statement about the code, CITE the exact file name where the evidence came from. 4. FORBIDDEN to infer implementations based only on Jira description or commit messages. 5. Always be absurdly HONEST and PRECISE in your analyses. 6. Write everything ALWAYS in ENGLISH, without exceptions. 7. IGNORE files like package.json, yarn.lock, .gitignore, etc for your implementation analysis. 8. **NEVER INVENT FILES OR CODE**. Use ONLY the provided files and commits as reference. ### DATA FOR ANALYSIS ### **Jira Description**: {truncatedJiraDescription} **Commits**: {truncatedCommits} **Modified Files**: {truncatedFiles} ### FINAL INSTRUCTION ### Analyze the commits and determine if Jira requirements were correctly implemented. Rigorously follow the rules above and generate a detailed technical report. **NEVER INVENT FILES OR CODE**. Use ONLY the provided information. ``` - Prompt sent to phi4-mini: ```ts ### CONTEXT ### You are an experienced software engineer responsible for creating clear, professional and well-formatted descriptions for Pull Requests (PRs) on GitHub. Your task is to transform a technical report into a PR description that is easy to understand and useful for reviewers (DEVs and QA). ### INSTRUCTIONS ### 1. **Markdown Format**: - Use Markdown format to structure the text. - **DO NOT use code blocks** (like ```markdown``` or ``````) to wrap Markdown. - Markdown should be directly renderable on GitHub. 2. **Tone and Style**: - Be technical, direct and professional. - Write in **ENGLISH** (no exceptions). - Use clear language and avoid unnecessary jargon. 3. **PR Structure**: - Follow typical Pull Request structure, including the following topics: - **PR Title**: A short and objective summary of changes. - **PR Description**: A detailed explanation of what was done. - **Motivation**: Why were these changes necessary? - **Changes Made**: List the main code changes. - **Impact**: What are the effects of these changes on the system? - **Recommendations for Reviewers**: Highlight specific points that need attention during review. 4. **Implementation Verification**: - If you **cannot confirm** that something was implemented based on the provided technical report, clearly indicate this in the PR. 5. **Highlight Main Points**: - Prioritize clarity and organization. - Include relevant technical details, but without being excessively verbose. 6. **Technical Report**: - Use the provided technical report as basis for generating the PR. ### TECHNICAL REPORT ### {codeAnalysis} ### FINAL INSTRUCTION ### Now, generate the PR description in Markdown format, following the structure and instructions provided above. **DO NOT use code blocks** to wrap Markdown. The text should be directly renderable on GitHub. ``` ## Ollama as an Ally To orchestrate the models, we used **Ollama**. It was fundamental in development for three reasons: - **Low latency in local tests**, accelerating prompt iterations. - **Flexibility in choosing and switching models**, without rewriting the backend. - **Simple API integration**, naturally fitting into the asynchronous flow. In the development phase, this agility made all the difference in quickly validating ideas.
Of course there are cons or, let's say, requirements: - **High machine configurations**, the computer will need robust configuration to handle running models in memory or GPU. - **Model configuration**, it will be necessary to configure temperature and adjust prompts point by point until it reaches a satisfactory response, as it is not a trained model like CHATGPT or Claude. ## Technical Challenges Not everything was smooth. Some points required adjustments: - **Rate limits** from GitHub and Jira APIs. - **Response consistency** from models, which needed extra validation. - **Asynchronous jobs** so the PR would be generated without blocking the application. Still, each decision brought learning about how to align AI with traditional software engineering. ## The Final Result With consolidated architecture and well-defined models, PRs stopped being a bottleneck. Today, each description brings **context, clarity and consistency**, reducing rework and increasing confidence of devs, reviewers and QAs. ## Conclusion More than generating automatic texts, this project showed how AI can become part of the **invisible infrastructure of productivity**. Separating models by function, integrating with everyday tools and orchestrating everything with Ollama is what transformed a bold idea into a practical solution. And most importantly: it opened space for developers to spend less time with bureaucracy and more time with **creation and innovation**.
